old: Ten cents from the East Caribbean States, dated 2004 — pocket money shared by eight Caribbean islands under one dollar and one central bank. The ship is the Golden Hind, the galleon Sir Francis Drake sailed around the world in the 1570s, drawn by Thomas Humphrey Paget; the crowned portrait of Queen Elizabeth the Second on the front is by Ian Rank-Broadley. This is the copper-nickel striking the islands used before switching to lighter steel coins in 2009, made for them at the Royal Mint in Britain. The collection already holds a 2004 strike of this coin recorded earlier from a shorthand note; this is the first one photographed on both sides.

old: An Australian 50 cents from 1977, struck for Queen Elizabeth the Second's Silver Jubilee — twenty-five years on the throne. It is a big twelve-sided coin. The front shows the young Queen in Arnold Machin's famous portrait, the one Australia used through the sixties and seventies. The back is a celebration wreath: a shining starburst in the middle ringed by small emblems, with the words SILVER JUBILEE and 50 CENTS around them. It was designed by Stuart Devlin, the goldsmith behind most of Australia's first decimal coins, and it was made to be kept — but plenty slipped into change anyway.

old: Ten cents from the East Caribbean States, dated 1991 — an older brother to the 2004 ten cents filed the same day (C348). The back is the same Golden Hind, Drake's little round-the-world galleon, with a 10 on each side. The front is what gives its age away: the Queen is young here, in Arnold Machin's portrait wearing a tiara, the likeness these islands used from the 1980s into the early 2000s before switching to the older crowned portrait. Eight Caribbean islands spend this one money, and coins like this crossed between them in every ferry and market stall. This one is copper-nickel, from the British Royal Mint years, heavier in the hand than the steel strikes that replaced it.

old: A big bronze ten centimes from the France of Napoleon the Third, dated 1867 — three years before his empire collapsed in the Franco-Prussian War. One side carries the Emperor's head wreathed in laurel, ringed by his name and title; the other shows the imperial eagle standing on a thunderbolt, the emblem Napoleon's regiments had carried into battle, with EMPIRE FRANCAIS above and DIX CENTIMES below between two stars. These heavy bronze pieces were the workhorse small change of France for decades — struck in the tens of millions, they stayed in pockets and tills into the next century, which is why so many survive as worn as this one.

old: One of Mexico's best-loved coin designs, struck in bronze from 1943: the Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan fills the reverse, its name carved at the pyramid's base, with the twin volcanoes Iztaccihuatl and Popocatepetl smoking behind it and a radiant Liberty cap dividing the big 20 overhead. Mexico authorized the type in August 1943, in the middle of the Second World War, to replace the silver twenty centavos it could no longer afford to strike - this is a first-year piece, one of some 46 million poured out that year. The obverse carries the national arms, the eagle on its cactus with the snake, and the words ESTADOS UNIDOS MEXICANOS.

old: A Heisei-era ten yen piece, dated in the eighth year of Emperor Akihito's reign - 1996. The obverse shows the Phoenix Hall of Byodo-in temple at Uji, its wing-like roofs spread over the water it was built beside in 1053; the reverse carries the big 10 inside an evergreen-oak wreath, with the era date written out in kanji below. The same design has been on Japan's ten yen since 1959 and still circulates today; this one joins the Heisei 14 (2002) specimen filed from a chat photo the same day.

old: A two rupees from the India of 2014, part of the series launched in 2011 to carry the rupee's new symbol - the sign that blends the Latin R with the Devanagari RA, adopted in 2010 to give the currency a mark of its own like the dollar or the pound. It sits above the big 2, with lotus flowers curling up both sides. The other face carries the Lion Capital of Ashoka, the four lions of the emperor's pillar that India took as its state emblem, with the country's name in Hindi on the left and English on the right and the motto Truth Alone Triumphs beneath. The small dot under the date marks it as a product of the Noida mint, outside Delhi.
